title: Exact Streaming Byte-Pair Tokenization with Rank-Ordered Two-Interval Compilation and Static Context Certificates
abstract: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is normally recomputed over an entire prefix whenever a stream grows, although consecutive prefixes differ by only one byte. We propose an exact incremental BPE transducer that maintains the canonical priority-ranked tokenization after every appended byte. Our central result is a rank-ordered successor-forest representation that compiles the complete ancestry-and-priority acceptance condition of every merge into at most two half-open depth-first-search intervals. We prove that the intervals can be constructed in $O(M+R)$ time by a single update-before-read rank sweep, where $M$ is the vocabulary size and $R$ is the number of merge rules, and that each runtime acceptance query consequently takes worst-case $O(1)$ time and four stored endpoints. We combine this representation with sound static context certificates, dense automaton transitions, and an atomic-state fast path. The resulting transducer is prefix-exact and uses $O(n+M+R+256S)$ space for a stream of length $n$ and an automaton with $S$ states. Randomized interleaved measurements on an ARM Cortex-X925 yield $3.232\pm0.660$ ms per 10 KB and a paired $3.97\times$ speedup over pointer traversal; an independent evaluation yields $3.462\pm0.827$ ms per 10 KB and $3.86\times$ paired speedup. The interval predicate alone becomes $2.05\times$ to $10.36\times$ faster than depth-dependent traversal as forest depth grows from 4 to 36. Across controlled deep-forest experiments, the integrated method is approximately $2.05\times$--$2.32\times$ faster than logarithmic centroid-search alternatives while preserving the batch BPE result at every tested prefix.
introduction:
Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is a foundational subword representation for neural language processing (Sennrich et al., 2015; Kudo and Richardson, 2018). In interactive generation, agent traces, editors, and network streams, an input grows one byte at a time. Retokenizing each complete prefix discards nearly all previous work. Exact incremental tokenization instead maintains the canonical batch result after every append, but it must respect globally ranked merges: recognizing that a vocabulary item ends at the current byte is insufficient because its left predecessor must be compatible with the merge priority.

We propose a cache-free incremental transducer based on a structural observation about the successor forest induced by BPE rules. If the children of every forest node are visited in increasing merge-rank order, then the children admissible for a candidate merge form a contiguous suffix of the node's depth-first interval. The exact predecessor condition is therefore the union of the predecessor singleton and one subtree suffix—at most two half-open intervals. This removes runtime child discovery, binary search, and depth-dependent pointer traversal from the acceptance predicate.

Our theoretical analysis establishes four results. First, we derive the exact prefix last-token criterion from ranked BPE semantics. Second, we prove the rank-ordered two-interval theorem. Third, we give a single forward sweep that constructs every cutoff in $O(M+R)$ time, including self-overlapping rules whose left and right operands coincide. Fourth, we prove that a context certificate may bypass the runtime predecessor lookup only when every vocabulary token compatible with that context lies in the candidate's acceptance intervals. These results yield worst-case $O(1)$ acceptance, $O(R)$ interval storage, and exact equality with canonical batch BPE at every prefix.

The implementation integrates four active mechanisms: two-interval acceptance, a dense 256-way suffix-automaton transition table, static context certificates, and a direct path for states containing only an atomic byte candidate. These mechanisms address different costs: intervals eliminate depth-dependent predicates; dense transitions eliminate failure-link walking; certificates eliminate proven-redundant predecessor reads; and the atomic path avoids candidate-loop overhead on common states.

Our experiments evaluate both isolated and integrated effects. In a forced predicate benchmark, interval acceptance improves from $2.05\times$ at depth 4 to $10.36\times$ at depth 36. In end-to-end deep-forest streams, it is approximately twice as fast as both component-weighted and unweighted centroid search. On the principal streaming workload, 76.99% of merge-state candidate pairs are statically certified, atomic states cover 80.0% of automaton states, and the corresponding fast path handles 60.94% of bytes. The complete method reduces paired latency by $8.095\pm0.680$ ms per 10 KB relative to pointer traversal while reproducing every tested prefix exactly.
related_work:
Sennrich et al. (2015) introduced BPE-derived subword units for open-vocabulary neural machine translation, establishing the practical motivation for merge-based tokenization. SentencePiece (Kudo and Richardson, 2018) made subword training and segmentation language-independent and applicable directly to raw text. Dagan et al. (2024) showed that vocabulary size, training data, and pre-tokenization materially affect generation speed, context utilization, and downstream quality. These works motivate efficient tokenization but do not provide a worst-case constant-time predicate for exact per-byte updates.

Zouhar et al. (2023) formalized BPE training as combinatorial optimization, established a curvature-dependent approximation guarantee for greedy vocabulary construction, and accelerated training. Berglund and van der Merwe (2023) formalized practical BPE semantics and investigated incremental and finite-state realizations. Our problem is complementary: the vocabulary and ranked rules are fixed, and we maintain their exact canonical segmentation at every byte prefix.

Jiang and Gong (2026) gave an exact incremental BPE algorithm with $O(\log^2 T)$ worst-case work per byte, where $T$ is maximum token length. Component-Weighted Centroid Search (Verma and Ying, 2026) weights branches by remaining component size and reduces this search to $O(\log T)$. We instead compile the predecessor-priority predicate into two intervals. Its query time is $O(1)$ independently of forest depth, and its $O(M+R)$ compilation is orthogonal to suffix recognition.

Aho and Corasick (1975) supplied the classical linear-time multiple-pattern matching automaton used to enumerate vocabulary suffixes. Kanda et al. (2022) studied engineering improvements for double-array Aho–Corasick layouts; our dense transition table follows the same objective of replacing irregular failure traversal with direct state transitions, while our contribution concerns exact BPE acceptance after recognition. Iwase et al. (2026) use the term prefix consistency for a reliability signal obtained by regenerating chain-of-thought continuations. Their statistical notion is unrelated to tokenization semantics; here prefix exactness means deterministic equality between incremental and canonical batch BPE for every byte prefix.

| Work | Mathematical formulation | Update/search complexity | Exact prefix guarantee | Distinguishing contribution |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Aho and Corasick (1975) | Multi-pattern finite automaton | $O(n+z)$ matching | No BPE guarantee | Simultaneous suffix recognition |
| Sennrich et al. (2015) | Greedy subword merges | Batch segmentation | Not incremental | BPE subwords for rare words |
| Kudo and Richardson (2018) | Raw-text subword model | Batch segmentation | Not incremental | Language-independent tokenization |
| Kanda et al. (2022) | Double-array pattern automaton | Linear scan | No BPE guarantee | Cache-conscious automaton engineering |
| Zouhar et al. (2023) | Submodular merge-sequence optimization | $O(N\log M)$ training | Not an update algorithm | Curvature-dependent training guarantee |
| Berglund and van der Merwe (2023) | Formal tokenizer semantics | Model-dependent | Formal incremental semantics | Finite-state and semantic analysis |
| Dagan et al. (2024) | Empirical tokenizer design | Batch/model-dependent | Not incremental | Downstream tokenizer ablations |
| Jiang and Gong (2026) | Incremental candidate-tree search | $O(\log^2 T)$ per byte | Yes | First strong worst-case incremental bound |
| Verma and Ying (2026) | Component-weighted centroid search | $O(\log T)$ per byte | Yes | Weighted logarithmic search |
| Iwase et al. (2026) | Regeneration-based reliability score | Sampling-dependent | Different notion | Reasoning-trace reliability |
| Ours | Rank-ordered forest intervals plus certified suffix states | $O(1)$ acceptance; $O(M+R)$ compilation | Yes | Two-interval priority predicate and certified bypass |
methodology:
### Problem formulation

Let $\Sigma=\{0,\ldots,255\}$ and let $\mathcal V=(v_0,\ldots,v_{M-1})$ contain the 256 byte atoms followed by $R=M-256$ merge tokens. Rule $r\in\{0,\ldots,R-1\}$ creates token $t_r=256+r$ from the ordered pair $(p(t_r),s(t_r))$. Its rank is $\rho(t_r)=r$, and its byte length satisfies $\ell(t_r)=\ell(p(t_r))+\ell(s(t_r))$. Canonical BPE repeatedly merges the adjacent available pair of minimum rank, breaking equal-position ambiguity from left to right.

For a byte prefix $x_{1:n}$, let $\Theta(x_{1:n})$ be its canonical tokenization and let $H[n]$ denote the final token of that tokenization. We store $H[0]=\bot$. Once all $H[j]$ are known, the complete segmentation is recovered by backtracking $n\leftarrow n-\ell(H[n])$.

Orient every merge token $t$ toward its right operand $s(t)$. Because operands precede the token that creates them, these edges form a forest rooted at byte atoms. Let $\operatorname{child}_a(k)$ be the first child of $a$ encountered on the path from descendant $k$ to $a$, when it exists.

**Lemma 1 (Prefix last-token criterion).** A recognized merge token $t$ ending at position $n$ is a valid final token exactly when $n>\ell(s(t))$ and, for $k=H[n-\ell(s(t))]$,

$$
 k=p(t)\quad\text{or}\quad
 \bigl(k\in\operatorname{Desc}(c),\ c=\operatorname{child}_{p(t)}(k),\ \rho(c)>\rho(t)\bigr).
$$

**Proof.** Split the spelling of $t$ immediately before its right operand. The suffix is exactly $s(t)$, while the tokenization of the preceding prefix ends in $k$. If $k=p(t)$, rule $t$ directly joins the boundary. Otherwise, $k$ can expose $p(t)$ at its right boundary only if repeated successor expansion reaches $p(t)$; equivalently, $k$ lies in the subtree of a child $c$ of $p(t)$. The merge producing $c$ crosses that exposed boundary. If $\rho(c)\le\rho(t)$, canonical BPE performs $c$ no later than $t$, so the boundary required by $t$ is unavailable. If $\rho(c)>\rho(t)$, rule $t$ has strictly higher priority and consumes the boundary before $c$ can do so. These cases are exhaustive because every path in the successor forest is unique. Hence the condition is necessary and sufficient. $\square$

### Rank-ordered interval compilation

Visit each forest node before its descendants and visit its children in increasing rank. Write $L_u$ and $R_u$ for the half-open DFS interval of $u$, so $k\in\operatorname{Desc}(u)$ iff $L_u\le L_k<R_u$.

**Theorem 1 (Two-interval theorem).** For every merge token $t$, there is a cutoff $q_t$ such that the complete acceptance set from Lemma 1 is

$$
\mathcal I_t=[L_{p(t)},L_{p(t)}+1)\ \cup\ [q_t,R_{p(t)}).
$$

Thus acceptance requires at most two interval tests and four integer endpoints.

**Proof.** The singleton interval contains exactly $p(t)$. The remaining valid tokens belong to child subtrees of $p(t)$ whose root rank exceeds $\rho(t)$. Children are visited in strictly increasing rank, and every child subtree is contiguous under DFS. Therefore all child subtrees of rank at most $\rho(t)$ concatenate into one prefix after the parent, while all child subtrees of greater rank concatenate into one suffix. Let $q_t$ be the first DFS position of that suffix, or $R_{p(t)}$ if it is empty. The suffix is exactly $[q_t,R_{p(t)})$. Combining it with the parent singleton proves the statement. $\square$

**Lemma 2 (Update-before-read cutoff recurrence).** Initialize $C[u]=L_u+1$. Processing rules in increasing rank, execute

$$C[s(t_r)]\leftarrow R_{t_r},\qquad q_{t_r}\leftarrow C[p(t_r)].$$

The resulting $q_{t_r}$ is the cutoff in Theorem 1, including when $p(t_r)=s(t_r)$.

**Proof.** Before rank $r$, $C[a]$ equals the right endpoint of the last child of $a$ having rank below $r$, or $L_a+1$ if no such child exists. This is true initially because no child has been processed. Token $t_r$ is a child of $s(t_r)$, and rank-ordered DFS places its subtree immediately after all earlier child subtrees; assigning $R_{t_r}$ therefore preserves the invariant for its parent. Reading $C[p(t_r)]$ then returns the first position after all children of $p(t_r)$ with rank at most $r$. The update must precede the read: if $p(t_r)=s(t_r)$, token $t_r$ itself is forbidden by the strict inequality and must already be included in the excluded prefix. Induction over $r$ proves the recurrence. $\square$

```text
Algorithm 1: Linear rank-ordered two-interval compilation
Input: ranked rules (p(t_r), s(t_r)), rank-ordered successor forest
Output: four endpoints for every merge token

1: Compute preorder intervals [L_u, R_u) by visiting children in increasing rank
2: for each vocabulary token u do
3:     C[u] <- L_u + 1
4: for r = 0, ..., R-1 do
5:     t <- 256 + r
6:     C[s(t)] <- R_t                 // update before read
7:     q <- C[p(t)]
8:     I[t] <- (L_p(t), L_p(t)+1, q, R_p(t))
9: return I
```

**Proposition 1 (Compilation complexity).** Algorithm 1 runs in $O(M+R)$ time and stores $4R$ endpoint integers in addition to the forest and DFS arrays.

**Proof.** Forest construction inserts one edge per merge, DFS visits each of the $M$ nodes and $R$ edges once, and the rank sweep performs constant work for each of the $R$ rules. No sorting is required because token creation order is rank order and children are inserted in that order. Each merge stores four endpoints. Therefore time is $O(M+R)$ and interval space is $O(R)$. $\square$

### Static certificates and streaming transduction

A suffix automaton reports every vocabulary item ending at the current byte. Candidates are ordered by decreasing byte length and then increasing merge rank, matching canonical final-token preference. For a candidate $t$ in automaton state $z$, define $W(z,t)$ as the vocabulary tokens that can end immediately before $s(t)$ under the suffix context represented by $z$. In the concrete construction, a conservative computable superset is all vocabulary spellings ending with the spelling of $p(t)$.

**Theorem 2 (Certificate soundness).** If $W(z,t)\subseteq\mathcal I_t$, then whenever state $z$ recognizes $t$ and the preceding prefix is nonempty, $t$ may be accepted without reading $H[n-\ell(s(t))]$.

**Proof.** Let $k=H[n-\ell(s(t))]$. By boundary compatibility, $k\in W(z,t)$. The certificate hypothesis gives $k\in\mathcal I_t$. Theorem 1 and Lemma 1 then imply that $t$ is valid. Because the certificate proves the same predicate used by dynamic acceptance, bypassing the lookup cannot alter the selected candidate. $\square$

A state whose output contains no merge candidate and at least one atomic candidate has a fixed byte-token result; it is handled directly. Other states inspect their ordered candidates. If a merge is not certified, the transducer reads the earlier last token and applies the two-interval predicate. The final byte candidate makes the candidate set total. A defensive byte assignment is retained if candidate enumeration is externally curtailed; under the complete suffix automaton it is unreachable because every state reached by a byte recognizes that byte suffix.

```text
Algorithm 2: Exact incremental append
Input: byte b, automaton state z, prefix length n, last-token array H
Output: final token of the extended prefix

1: z <- DenseTransition[z, b]; n <- n + 1
2: if z is atomic-only then
3:     H[n] <- AtomicToken[z]; return H[n]
4: for candidate t in outputs(z), ordered by decreasing length then rank do
5:     if t is an atomic byte then
6:         H[n] <- t; return t
7:     d <- length(s(t))
8:     if n <= d then continue
9:     if Certificate[z,t] then
10:        H[n] <- t; return t
11:    k <- H[n-d]; x <- L_k
12:    (a,b0,q,e) <- I[t]
13:    if (a <= x < b0) or (q <= x < e) then
14:        H[n] <- t; return t
15: H[n] <- b; return b
```

**Theorem 3 (Prefix exactness).** After every append at position $n$, Algorithm 2 returns the final token of $\Theta(x_{1:n})$; backtracking through token lengths returns all of $\Theta(x_{1:n})$.

**Proof.** Proceed by induction on $n$. The empty prefix is trivial. Assume $H[j]$ is correct for every $j<n$. The suffix automaton enumerates all vocabulary tokens ending at $n$. By Lemma 1 and Theorem 1, every dynamic interval decision is valid exactly when the corresponding token can be the canonical final token. Theorem 2 shows that certified decisions are equivalent to those dynamic decisions. Candidate ordering selects the canonical valid final token, and an atomic byte always exists. Hence $H[n]$ is correct. Removing its $\ell(H[n])$ bytes exposes an earlier prefix whose stored final token is correct by induction; repeated removal reconstructs the entire canonical segmentation. $\square$

**Proposition 2 (Runtime and space).** With precomputed dense transitions, each automaton transition and each acceptance predicate takes $O(1)$ time. If $c_z$ candidates are inspected in state $z$, append time is $O(c_z)$ and is $O(1)$ whenever the per-state candidate bound is fixed. Reconstruction takes $O(m)$ for an output of $m$ tokens. For a length-$n$ stream, total space is $O(n+M+R+256S+P)$, where $S$ is the number of automaton states and $P$ is the number of stored state-candidate pairs.

**Proof.** A dense transition is one indexed array access; interval acceptance performs a constant number of indexed reads and comparisons. Candidate inspection is linear only in the state's output list. The last-token history stores $n+1$ entries, forest and interval structures use $O(M+R)$ space, the transition table contains $256S$ entries, and candidate metadata uses $O(P)$. Backtracking emits one token per iteration. $\square$
experiments:
### Experimental protocol

We evaluate exact incremental tokenization on multilingual prose and source-code byte streams. Every byte prefix is compared with an independent global greedy BPE implementation. Latency is measured in seven randomized interleaved paired passes for the principal studies and five passes for controlled forest sweeps. We report sample means with two-sided Student-$t$ 95% confidence-interval half-widths. All principal measurements use one pinned ARM Cortex-X925 core at 3.90 GHz with Python 3.12.3. The primary vocabulary contains 328 tokens, 72 merges, maximum token length 6 bytes, 370 suffix-automaton states, and successor-forest depth 4.

### Streaming latency and exactness

| Evaluation | Bytes/prefixes | Ours (ms/10 KB) | Pointer traversal (ms/10 KB) | Paired reduction (ms) | Speedup | Exact prefixes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Principal stream | 2,304 | $3.232\pm0.660$ | 11.332 | $8.095\pm0.680$ | $3.97\times$ | 100% |
| Independent stream | 2,304 | $3.462\pm0.827$ | 11.321 | $7.875\pm0.679$ | $3.86\times$ | 100% |

The paired intervals are strictly positive: their lower endpoints are 7.415 and 7.196 ms per 10 KB, respectively. Thus the integrated speedup is not explained by pass-to-pass timing drift. The principal construction cost is 20.11 ms versus 0.65 ms for pointer traversal, giving an estimated streaming break-even point of 22.94 KB. Peak traced memory is 941,064 bytes, and complete token reconstruction costs 61.7 microseconds.

### Static certificates and fast-path telemetry

| Mechanism statistic | Principal stream | Independent stream |
|---|---:|---:|
| Atomic-only automaton states | 296 / 370 (80.00%) | 296 / 370 (80.00%) |
| Certified merge candidate pairs | 87 / 113 (76.99%) | 87 / 113 (76.99%) |
| Atomic-path byte hits | 1,404 / 2,304 (60.94%) | 1,396 / 2,304 (60.59%) |
| Certificate hits among merge-state bytes | 644 / 900 (71.56%) | 633 / 908 (69.71%) |
| Dynamic interval evaluations | 289 | 308 |
| Prefix equivalence | 100% | 100% |

Static analysis removes most dynamic predecessor checks: only 289 and 308 interval evaluations remain across 2,304 bytes. The close certification and hit rates across the two streams show that the certificates capture structural context rather than a single byte sequence. Atomic dispatch handles roughly three fifths of all bytes before candidate iteration.

### Component subtraction and mechanism isolation

| Variant | Mean ms/10 KB | Change from full method (ms) | Paired 95% CI | Mechanism interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Full method | 2.6665 | 0.0000 | $\pm0.0000$ | All four mechanisms |
| Without static certificates | 2.7813 | +0.1148 | $\pm0.2780$ | More dynamic interval reads |
| Pointer predicate with certificates | 2.7518 | +0.0853 | $\pm0.1233$ | Certificates mask many predicate calls |
| Pointer predicate without certificates | 3.7590 | +1.0925 | $\pm0.2279$ | Full depth-dependent traversal cost |
| Without atomic-state dispatch | 3.0902 | +0.4237 | $\pm0.2559$ | Candidate-loop overhead restored |
| Without dense transitions | 3.8791 | +1.2126 | $\pm0.4392$ | Failure-link traversal restored |
| Explicit predecessor sets | 4.3845 | +1.7180 | $\pm0.3336$ | Hash membership and larger representation |

Dense transitions and atomic dispatch have strictly positive paired lower bounds of 0.773 and 0.168 ms, respectively. Replacing intervals with uncached pointer traversal also has a strictly positive 0.865 ms lower bound when certificates are removed. Certificates reduce the mean latency by 0.115 ms and reduce dynamic predicate traffic substantially, although this isolated timing interval crosses zero. The $2\times2$ interval-by-certificate analysis measures an interval saving of $0.978\pm0.154$ ms without certificates, $0.085\pm0.123$ ms with certificates, and a positive interaction contrast of $0.892\pm0.232$ ms. This is the expected mechanism: successful certificates bypass either predicate, so the interval advantage concentrates on uncertified states.

### Controlled fixed-vocabulary depth sweep

| Forest depth | Interval ms/10 KB | Weighted centroid | Unweighted centroid | Predicate speedup | Set/interval storage ratio | Exact prefixes |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 2.1176 | 4.7268 | 4.9141 | $2.10\times$ | $1.48\times$ | 100% |
| 12 | 1.8962 | 4.0005 | 4.0733 | $4.06\times$ | $2.05\times$ | 100% |
| 24 | 1.8522 | 3.8207 | 3.8759 | $6.92\times$ | $2.30\times$ | 100% |
| 36 | 1.8419 | 3.7797 | 3.8478 | $10.36\times$ | $2.40\times$ | 100% |

This sweep holds the number of merges fixed at 320 and varies only successor-forest depth. The forced predicate advantage rises monotonically from $2.10\times$ to $10.36\times$, directly confirming the theoretical separation between constant-time interval membership and depth-dependent traversal. End-to-end latency remains nearly flat as depth increases, whereas the method is $2.05\times$--$2.32\times$ faster than the two centroid-search implementations. Interval storage remains fixed at 640 interval units while explicit-set occupancy grows from 944 to 1,536 entries.

### Multi-scale deep-forest sweep

| Merges | Depth | Interval ms/10 KB | Weighted centroid | Jiang–Gong search | Predicate speedup | Exact prefixes |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 72 | 4 | 2.0611 | 4.7018 | 4.7865 | $2.05\times$ | 100% |
| 160 | 12 | 1.8395 | 3.9441 | 4.0824 | $3.97\times$ | 100% |
| 320 | 24 | 1.8323 | 3.7673 | 3.8265 | $6.90\times$ | 100% |
| 512 | 36 | 1.8523 | 3.8233 | 3.8303 | $9.78\times$ | 100% |

Across vocabularies containing 328 to 768 tokens, interval latency stays between 1.832 and 2.061 ms per 10 KB despite a ninefold increase in forest depth. Relative to Component-Weighted Centroid Search, the end-to-end speedup is $2.06\times$--$2.28\times$; relative to Jiang and Gong, it is $2.07\times$--$2.32\times$. Explicit-set occupancy grows from 264 to 2,653 entries, whereas the two-interval representation grows linearly from 144 to 1,024 units, increasing the observed storage reduction from $1.83\times$ to $2.59\times$. All prefixes in every scale and depth condition match canonical batch BPE.
limitations:
The dense transition table deliberately exchanges memory for predictable transition latency, requiring $256S$ entries; compressed or double-array layouts may be preferable for substantially larger automata or memory-constrained deployment. The last-token history is linear in stream length because arbitrary reconstruction is supported. Applications that emit irrevocable tokens could combine the method with a proven eager-output boundary and discard older history.

The static certificate test uses a conservative boundary-compatible vocabulary superset. It is sound but not necessarily complete, so some states still execute the interval predicate even when a stronger context analysis could prove acceptance. Certificate compilation also contributes to initialization cost, making short streams slower in total wall time until roughly 23 KB in the measured implementation.

The reported systems measurements use a Python implementation on one ARM processor, a compact learned vocabulary, and synthetic depth-controlled forests. The asymptotic predicate and exactness results are architecture-independent, but absolute latency, cache behavior, and construction trade-offs should be measured in optimized native implementations and with production-scale vocabularies. Finally, the method assumes a canonical acyclic ranked BPE vocabulary in which operands precede the token they create; tokenizers with context-dependent normalization, stochastic segmentation, or noncanonical duplicate spellings require separate semantic treatment.
